entry: City, capital of [[Bashkortostan]], Russia, on the Ufa Plateau west of the southern [[Ural Mountains]]. The city lies at the confluence of the Belaya and Ufa rivers and has over 1.1 million residents, making it the tenth-most populous city in Russia. Founded as a fortress in 1574 on the orders of [[Ivan the Terrible]], it became capital of Ufa Governorate in 1865. Its economy rests on oil refining, chemicals and mechanical engineering, and the petroleum company Bashneft is headquartered there. The population is ethnically diverse, with substantial Bashkir and [[Tatars|Tatar]] communities alongside an ethnic Russian majority. Several institutions, including Bashkir State University, are located in the city, which hosted separate summits of the [[BRICS]] group and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in 2015.

Art museum in [[Florence]], Italy, adjacent to the Piazza della Signoria. Construction of the complex began in 1560 under [[Giorgio Vasari]], commissioned by Cosimo I de' Medici to house Florentine administrative offices, which gave the building its name, from *uffizi*, "offices." It was completed in 1581, and its top floor became a gallery for the [[House of Medici|Medici]] collection. After the demise of the Medici, their collections passed to the city under a family pact negotiated by Anna Maria Luisa de' Medici, the last Medici heiress. The museum opened to the public in 1769 and was formally registered in 1865. Its Italian Renaissance collection is among the most important in the world, including *The Birth of Venus* by [[Sandro Botticelli|Botticelli]]. With over two million visitors in 2016, it was the most visited art gallery in Italy.

Landlocked country in [[East Africa]] (pop., 2024: 45.9 million). Uganda is named after the Buganda kingdom, and its official languages are English and [[Swahili]]. Bantu and Nilotic groups arrived about 3,000 years ago, and Britain established the Protectorate of Uganda in 1894. Uganda gained independence in 1962 with Milton Obote as prime minister. [[Idi Amin]] seized power in a 1971 coup and ruled as a brutal dictator until 1979. After a six-year guerrilla war, the National Resistance Movement of Yoweri Museveni took power in 1986, and Museveni has led the country since. Political oppression, corruption and electoral fraud allegations persist, though literacy has improved and HIV infection has been reduced. The capital and largest city is [[Kampala]]. Lake Victoria, the world's second-largest freshwater lake, lies in the south.

Ancient Levantine port city in northern [[Syria]], about 10 km north of Latakia. Occupied from the 8th millennium BC, it reached its height from about 1450 to 1185 BC as a mercantile kingdom trading with Egypt, [[Cyprus]], Minoan [[Crete]] and the [[Hittites]], to whom it was at times a vassal state. Its scribes wrote in Ugaritic, a Northwest Semitic language, using an alphabetic cuneiform script that is the oldest known systematic alphabet. The city was destroyed around 1185 BC, during the [[Late Bronze Age collapse]]. Its archives, including the Baal Cycle of myths, shed light on Canaanite religion and language. Discovered in 1928 at the site known in Arabic as Ras Shamra, the city has yielded over 1,400 clay tablets.

Genre of Japanese art that flourished from the 17th through 19th centuries, producing woodblock prints and paintings of beautiful women, [[Kabuki]] actors, sumo wrestlers and landscapes. Its name means "pictures of the floating world," a term for the urban pleasure districts of Edo, now Tokyo, which became the seat of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] in 1603. Prints were the main form, made by a team of designer, carver, printer and publisher, and full-color printing became standard in the 1760s. The 19th-century masters [[Hokusai]] and [[Hiroshige]] produced landscapes including *The Great Wave off Kanagawa*. After the [[Meiji Restoration]] the genre declined, but its influence on Western artists such as [[Edgar Degas]] and [[Vincent van Gogh]] made it central to Western perceptions of Japanese art.

Country in [[Eastern Europe]], the second-largest country in Europe after [[Russia]]. Its capital and largest city is [[Kyiv]]. It covers 603,628 sq km (230,000 sq mi) and has about 32 million people. The [[Kievan Rus']] state, which emerged in the 9th century, was the largest realm in Europe in the 10th and 11th centuries. Later ruled by Lithuanian, Polish, Ottoman and Russian powers, Ukraine became a constituent republic of the [[Soviet Union]] in 1922 and gained independence in 1991. Millions died in the [[Holodomor]], a human-made famine of the early 1930s, and 7 million civilians were killed during World War II. After the 2014 Euromaidan revolution, Russia annexed the Crimean Peninsula, and the 2022 Russian invasion began a new phase of war. Ukraine is a semi-presidential republic and a founding member of the [[United Nations]].

East Slavic language, the native tongue of most Ukrainians and spoken primarily in [[Ukraine]]. It is written in a variant of the [[Cyrillic script]] with 33 letters, and it shares more mutual intelligibility with Belarusian than with [[Russian language|Russian]]. Ukrainian descends from Old East Slavic, the language of Kievan Rus'. In the [[Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] the language developed as Ruthenian, and by the 18th century regional variants had formed the basis of modern Ukrainian. Russification banned it from schools and as a language of instruction in the Russian Empire, and Soviet policies also curtailed its use, but it remained particularly strong in western Ukraine. Writers such as [[Taras Shevchenko]] helped make it a vehicle of national identity.

Capital and largest city of [[Mongolia]], in a valley on the Tuul River at about 1,300 metres (4,300 ft). It is the coldest capital in the world by average yearly temperature. Founded in 1639 as a nomadic [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] monastery, the settlement moved 29 times before it was permanently settled on its present site in 1778. As Örgöö, or Urga, it became Mongolia's leading religious center. Independence efforts followed the collapse of the [[Qing dynasty]] in 1911. When the city became capital of the Mongolian People's Republic in 1924, it was renamed Ulaanbaatar, "Red Hero." Migration since 1990 has caused rapid growth, and coal heating in its ger districts produces [[Air pollution|air pollution]] that ranks among the world's worst. With just over 1.6 million residents as of December 2022, it holds almost half of Mongolia's population.

Long-term inflammatory bowel disease causing inflammation and ulcers in the colon and rectum. It is one of two main types of inflammatory bowel disease, the other being [[Crohn's disease]]. Active disease typically causes diarrhea mixed with blood and abdominal pain, with weight loss and fever possible, in flares separated by remission. The cause is unknown. Diagnosis is typically by [[Endoscopy|colonoscopy]] with tissue biopsies. Treatment uses aminosalicylates, steroids, immunosuppressants and biologics. Surgical removal of the colon and rectum generally cures the condition; it is needed if the disease is severe, unresponsive to treatment, or complicated by [[Colorectal cancer|colon cancer]].

Traditional province in the north of [[Ireland]], made up of nine counties. Six of them form [[Northern Ireland]], part of the United Kingdom, and three are in the [[Republic of Ireland]]. It is the second-largest of Ireland's four provinces, with [[Belfast]] its largest city, and almost half its population is Protestant. Ulster was the most Gaelic and independent of Ireland's provinces until its rulers were defeated in the Nine Years' War. King James I then settled Scottish and English Protestants in the Plantation of Ulster. The Government of Ireland Act of 1920 created Northern Ireland from six Ulster counties.

American [[Mixed martial arts|mixed martial arts]] (MMA) promotion company based in the [[Las Vegas]] area of Nevada. It is the largest MMA promotion, with over 578 fighters across 11 weight divisions. The first event was held in 1993 in [[Denver]], Colorado, as a tournament with minimal rules. Later events adopted weight classes and the Unified Rules of Mixed Martial Arts. Dana White has been president since 2001 and CEO since 2023. The company merged with [[WWE]] in 2023 to form TKO Group Holdings. In 2025 it signed a seven-year deal worth US$7.7 billion with Paramount Skydance, operator of [[CBS]], and left pay-per-view.

Theories about the long-term future of the universe, a question in [[Physical cosmology|physical cosmology]]. Observations by [[Edwin Hubble]] showed galaxies moving apart, supporting the [[Big Bang]] theory that the universe began very dense about 13.787 billion years ago. Its ultimate fate depends on its shape and on the amounts of [[Dark matter|dark matter]] and [[Dark energy|dark energy]] it contains. Cosmologists strongly agree that the universe is flat and will expand forever. The theory of general relativity, developed by [[Albert Einstein]] in 1915, allows several solutions, each implying a different fate. In a closed universe, gravity would halt expansion in a [[Big Crunch]]. Planck 2018 data indicate that ordinary matter makes up about 5% of the universe, dark matter about 25% and dark energy approximately 70%, with accelerated expansion that could end in a cold "heat death" as stars burn out.

Deep blue pigment historically made by grinding the mineral lazurite from [[Lapis lazuli]] and washing it through a complex process. The name comes from Latin *ultramarinus*, "beyond the sea," because Italian traders imported the stone from mines in [[Afghanistan]] in the 14th and 15th centuries, with [[Venice]] a major center of distribution. Among the finest and most costly pigments of the [[Renaissance]], it was used for the robes of the Virgin Mary and was at times valued as highly as gold. Synthetic ultramarine, first developed in 1826, made the pigment widely available. It is generally permanent under stable conditions.

Sound with frequencies above 20 kilohertz, the approximate upper limit of human hearing. Ultrasonic devices operate from 20 kHz up to several gigahertz. In medicine, ultrasound imaging, or [[Medical imaging|sonography]], is widely used because it involves no [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing radiation]]. Industry uses it to detect hidden flaws in products and structures, and to clean, mix and accelerate chemical processes. [[Bat|Bats]] and [[Porpoise|porpoises]] use ultrasound to locate prey and obstacles, and echolocation in bats was discovered by Lazzaro Spallanzani in 1794. [[Francis Galton]] invented an ultrasonic whistle in 1893 to measure animal hearing. During the First World War, Paul Langevin built an ultrasound transducer that used the [[Piezoelectricity|piezoelectric]] effect to detect submerged objects.

Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths of 100–400 nanometers, shorter than visible light. Ultraviolet makes up about 10% of the total electromagnetic output of the [[Sun]]. Its photons carry enough energy to break chemical bonds and damage [[DNA]], which is why UV sterilizes surfaces, causes sunburn and raises the risk of [[Skin cancer]]. Ozone and molecular oxygen absorb most sunlight below about 300 nm, but UVB is needed by most land vertebrates, including humans, to form [[Vitamin D]]. Mercury-vapor and tanning lamps also emit UV. Johann Wilhelm Ritter discovered it in February 1801 when invisible rays beyond the violet end of the spectrum darkened silver chloride paper. Insects, birds and some mammals can see near-UV.

Timurid sultan, astronomer and mathematician. The grandson of [[Timur]], he was governor of [[Samarkand]] from 1409 and named sovereign ruler of Mavarannahr in 1411, and he made the city an intellectual center by building a madrasa there between 1417 and 1420. He built the Ulugh Beg Observatory in Samarkand between 1424 and 1429, considered one of the finest in the [[Islam|Islamic]] world and the largest in [[Central Asia]]. Lacking telescopes, he used a huge sextant to improve accuracy. His *Zij-i Sultani* (1437) catalogued 1,018 stars with accurate positions. His scientific achievements were not matched by his political skill, and he was overthrown and assassinated by his son, Abd al-Latif, after a short reign.

Large sandstone monolith in the [[Northern Territory]] of Australia, also known as Ayers Rock. It stands 348 m (1,142 ft) high and reaches 863 m (2,831 ft) above sea level, and its reddish color derives from iron oxide in the rock. It lies about 335 km south-west of [[Alice Springs]] and is sacred to the Pitjantjatjara Aṉangu people, who lead tours explaining their stories and bush knowledge. Uluru and nearby Kata Tjuta form Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, a [[World Heritage Site]]. Europeans first mapped the formation in 1872, and William Gosse named it Ayers Rock in 1873. A dual name was adopted in 1993, and climbing was banned in 2019 because of its sacred status.

[[American Civil War|Civil War]] general and 18th [[President of the United States|president of the United States]], serving 1869–1877. Born in Ohio, Grant graduated from the [[United States Military Academy]] and served in the Mexican–American War before leaving the army in 1854. As a Union general he led the Vicksburg campaign in 1863, giving the Union control of the Mississippi River, and in 1865 he accepted [[Robert E. Lee]]'s surrender at Appomattox. As president he supported Reconstruction and the Fifteenth Amendment, prosecuted the [[Ku Klux Klan]] and helped create the [[United States Department of Justice|Department of Justice]]. His administration was marred by corruption scandals, and his response to the Panic of 1873 did not halt the Long Depression. Dying of throat cancer, he wrote memoirs that became a major financial success for his family.

Modernist novel by the Irish writer [[James Joyce]], published in full in Paris in 1922. Partly serialized in *The Little Review* from 1918 to 1920, it follows three Dubliners through a single day, June 16, 1904, which fans celebrate as Bloomsday. The setting is [[Dublin]], and its characters parallel [[Odysseus]] and the figures of [[Homer]]'s *Odyssey*: Leopold Bloom corresponds to Odysseus, Molly Bloom to Penelope and Stephen Dedalus to Telemachus. Written in stream-of-consciousness technique, with puns, parodies and allusions, the novel is regarded as one of the most important works of modernist literature. An obscenity trial in the United States in 1921 and later bans made it controversial until a 1933 federal court ruling declared it non-obscene.

American actress known for her collaborations with [[Quentin Tarantino]]. She gained international attention as Mia Wallace in *Pulp Fiction* (1994), earning an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress. As the Bride in *Kill Bill: Volume 1* and *Volume 2*, she received a BAFTA Award nomination. Thurman won a Golden Globe for the [[HBO]] film *Hysterical Blindness* and has also appeared in *Gattaca* and *Les Misérables*. She made her Broadway debut in *The Parisian Woman*. Thurman has [[Dyslexia|dyslexia]] and has spoken openly about it.

One of the five basic tastes, savory or brothy, produced mainly by glutamates and nucleotides. Umami is found in meats, fish, [[Tomato|tomatoes]], mushrooms, [[Soy sauce]] and cheeses such as Parmesan. In 1908 Kikunae Ikeda of the [[University of Tokyo]] identified it as a distinct taste attributed to glutamic acid. In 1909 he co-founded Ajinomoto, which marketed the first umami seasoning, [[Monosodium glutamate|monosodium glutamate]] (MSG). Umami receptors were identified on the tongue in 2000. The name is Japanese, meaning roughly "pleasant savory taste."

Second [[Rashidun Caliphate|Rashidun]] caliph, ruling 634–644. A senior companion and father-in-law of the Prophet [[Muhammad]], he initially opposed him, then converted to Islam in 616 and became the first Muslim to pray openly at the [[Kaaba]]. He succeeded [[Abu Bakr]] as caliph. During his rule the caliphate expanded rapidly: his armies conquered the [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian]] Persian Empire and more than two-thirds of the [[Byzantine Empire]]. He introduced the Hijri calendar and lifted the Christian ban on Jews entering [[Jerusalem]]. He is revered in Sunni Islam as a just ruler, while [[Shia Islam|Shia Islam]] views him negatively. He was assassinated by a Persian slave.

Second Islamic caliphate, ruled by the Umayyad dynasty from 661 to 750 from [[Damascus]]. It succeeded the [[Rashidun Caliphate]] when [[Mu'awiya I|Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan]], governor of Syria, became caliph after the First Fitna, and it was the first hereditary caliphate. Under [[Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan|Abd al-Malik]] the state centralized power, Arabized its bureaucracy and built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. Conquests reached the [[Maghreb]], the Iberian Peninsula, Central Asia and Sindh, and at its greatest extent the caliphate covered 11,000,000–15,000,000 sq km. Privilege for Arabs and discrimination against non-Arab converts, along with constant warfare, fueled revolts. The Abbasids overthrew the dynasty in 750, but [[Abd al-Rahman I]] escaped to found a new state in [[Al-Andalus|al-Andalus]].

Arab Islamic state in Iberia, ruled by the Umayyad dynasty from 756 to 1031 and centered on Córdoba. It was founded by [[Abd al-Rahman I]], an Umayyad prince who fled Syria after the [[Abbasid Caliphate|Abbasid]] revolution, and it controlled most of the Iberian Peninsula, known to Muslims as [[Al-Andalus]], as well as the [[Balearic Islands]] and parts of North Africa. [[Abd al-Rahman III]] proclaimed himself caliph in 929. The state flourished for nearly three centuries, with expanded trade and culture, including the Great Mosque of Córdoba and the palatine city of Madinat al-Zahra. Raids reached [[Corsica]] in 806. A civil war, the Fitna of al-Andalus, fractured the state in the early 11th century, and in 1031 it split into independent taifa kingdoms.

Italian medievalist, philosopher, [[Semiotics|semiotician]] and novelist, best known for *The Name of the Rose* (1980). Born in Alessandria, Piedmont, he wrote his thesis on the aesthetics of [[Thomas Aquinas]] at the University of Turin and later taught for much of his life at the [[University of Bologna]]. His 1980 historical mystery combined semiotics, biblical analysis and medieval studies, and *Foucault's Pendulum* (1988) explored the history of occultism. From 1985 he wrote a twice-monthly column, *La Bustina di Minerva*, for the magazine *L'Espresso*. His 1995 essay "Ur-Fascism" lists fourteen properties of [[Fascism|fascist]] ideologies. His *A Theory of Semiotics* (1975) became a foundational text in the field.
